question: Under the common-law 'mirror image rule' of contract formation, a purported acceptance that changes or adds terms to the offer is treated as:
choice_a: A counteroffer and a rejection of the original offer, not a valid acceptance
choice_b: A valid acceptance of the original offer, with the new terms simply ignored
choice_c: An automatic breach of contract by the offeree
choice_d: A binding contract on the original offeror's terms only
explanation: Under the mirror image rule, an acceptance must match the terms of the offer exactly; a response that varies or adds terms operates as a counteroffer, which rejects and terminates the original offer and puts a new offer on the table for the original offeror to accept, reject, or counter in turn.
source_note: General contract law -- mirror image rule, well-corroborated

question: As a general rule of contract law, an offeror who has made an offer but not yet received acceptance:
choice_a: May revoke the offer at any time before it is accepted, unless the offer is irrevocable (such as a firm option supported by separate consideration)
choice_b: May never revoke the offer once it has been communicated to the offeree
choice_c: Must wait a minimum of 30 days before revoking any offer
choice_d: May revoke the offer only with the consent of a court
explanation: At common law, an offeror generally retains the power to revoke an offer at any time before it is accepted, since no contract yet exists; an important exception applies to an option contract, where the offeree has paid separate consideration for the offeror's promise to hold the offer open, making it irrevocable for the stated period.
source_note: General contract law -- revocation of offers, well-corroborated

question: Under the common-law 'mailbox rule,' when an offeree accepts an offer by mail using an authorized method of communication, the acceptance generally becomes effective:
choice_a: Upon proper dispatch (mailing) of the acceptance, not upon the offeror's actual receipt of it
choice_b: Only once the offeror physically opens and reads the letter
choice_c: Only after 10 business days have passed
choice_d: Never, because mailed acceptances are unenforceable
explanation: The mailbox rule provides that an acceptance sent by an authorized means of communication is effective upon dispatch, rather than upon the offeror's receipt -- though many standardized real estate contracts, including the FAR/BAR forms, modify this default rule by requiring actual delivery of the signed acceptance to establish the contract's effective date.
source_note: General contract law -- mailbox rule, well-corroborated

question: Regarding the adequacy of consideration needed to form a valid contract, courts generally:
choice_a: Refuse to inquire into whether the bargained-for consideration was adequate or a good deal, so long as legally sufficient consideration exists on both sides
choice_b: Require that each party's consideration be of exactly equal monetary value
choice_c: Void any contract where one party paid less than fair market value
choice_d: Require a licensed appraiser to certify the value exchanged before a contract can be valid
explanation: Courts generally do not weigh the adequacy (relative economic value) of consideration exchanged by the parties, only whether legally sufficient consideration exists on each side; parties are free to make a good or bad bargain, and gross inadequacy of price alone is not ordinarily grounds to invalidate an otherwise properly formed contract (though it may be evidence of fraud, duress, or unconscionability in some cases).
source_note: General contract law -- adequacy vs. sufficiency of consideration, well-corroborated

question: For an option contract to be irrevocable and binding on the property owner (optionor) during the option period, the optionee must generally provide:
choice_a: Separate, independent consideration paid specifically for the option right itself, distinct from the eventual purchase price
choice_b: Nothing at all, since options are gratuitous by definition
choice_c: A promise to purchase the property no matter what
choice_d: A recorded deed transferring equitable title immediately
explanation: Because an option is itself a contract, it requires its own consideration -- typically a sum of money paid to the optionor in exchange for the optionor's promise to hold the offer open -- separate from the purchase price that would be paid if the option is later exercised; without such separate option consideration, the optionor's promise to hold the offer open is generally not binding and could be revoked like an ordinary offer.
source_note: General contract law -- option contract consideration, well-corroborated

question: A contract entered into by a minor (a person who has not reached the age of legal majority) is generally treated as:
choice_a: Voidable at the minor's election -- the minor may disaffirm it, while the adult party generally remains bound
choice_b: Void from the outset and incapable of ever being enforced by anyone
choice_c: Automatically ratified once the minor turns 18, with no action required
choice_d: Fully enforceable against the minor exactly as if the minor were an adult
explanation: A minor generally lacks full legal capacity to contract, making most contracts entered into by a minor voidable at the minor's election -- the minor may disaffirm (rescind) the contract, generally either during minority or within a reasonable time after reaching majority -- while the adult contracting party typically remains bound unless the minor elects to void it.
source_note: General contract law -- minors' capacity to contract, well-corroborated

question: A contract entered into by a person who has been formally adjudicated by a court to be mentally incompetent is generally treated as:
choice_a: Void, since a judicially adjudicated incompetent lacks the legal capacity to contract at all
choice_b: Fully valid and binding, identical to a contract with any competent adult
choice_c: Voidable only at the election of the other, competent party
choice_d: Automatically reformed by a court to reflect fair terms
explanation: A contract made by a person who has already been judicially adjudicated incompetent is generally void, not merely voidable, because that person has been formally determined by a court to lack legal capacity; this differs from a person who is not yet adjudicated but who lacked the mental capacity to understand the transaction at the time of contracting, whose contract is typically treated as voidable rather than void.
source_note: General contract law -- capacity of adjudicated incompetents, well-corroborated

question: A 'mutual mistake' that may justify rescission of a real estate contract occurs when:
choice_a: Both parties share the same erroneous belief about a material fact existing at the time the contract was formed, such that the contract does not reflect what either party actually intended
choice_b: One party simply changes their mind after signing
choice_c: Only the buyer, but not the seller, is mistaken about a fact
choice_d: The seller intentionally lies about the property's condition
explanation: A mutual mistake exists when both contracting parties are mistaken about the same material fact at the time of contracting, such that the resulting agreement fails to reflect what either party genuinely believed or intended -- a recognized basis for rescission, distinct from a unilateral mistake (where only one party is mistaken) or fraud (an intentional misstatement).
source_note: General contract law -- mutual mistake, well-corroborated

question: A 'unilateral mistake,' where only one contracting party is mistaken about a material fact, generally:
choice_a: Does not excuse the mistaken party's performance, unless the other party knew or should have known of the mistake, or enforcement would be unconscionable
choice_b: Automatically voids the contract regardless of the other party's knowledge or conduct
choice_c: Has no legal significance whatsoever under any circumstances
choice_d: Entitles the mistaken party to automatic punitive damages
explanation: Unlike a mutual mistake shared by both parties, a unilateral mistake by only one party generally does not by itself excuse that party's performance or void the contract, because the non-mistaken party is otherwise entitled to rely on the agreement as made -- relief is typically available only in narrower circumstances, such as where the other party knew or should have known of the error, or where enforcing the contract as written would be unconscionable.
source_note: General contract law -- unilateral mistake, well-corroborated

question: To establish fraudulent misrepresentation sufficient to rescind a real estate contract or recover damages, a party must generally prove:
choice_a: A false statement of material fact, knowledge of its falsity (or reckless disregard for the truth), intent to induce reliance, justifiable reliance by the other party, and resulting damage
choice_b: Only that the final sale price was higher than the buyer wanted to pay
choice_c: That the seller used a real estate agent rather than selling by owner
choice_d: That the contract was not notarized
explanation: Fraudulent misrepresentation generally requires proof of a false statement of material fact, the speaker's knowledge of its falsity or reckless disregard for the truth, an intent to induce the other party's reliance, justifiable reliance by that party, and resulting damage -- a higher bar than mere negligent or innocent misstatement.
source_note: General contract/tort law -- elements of fraudulent misrepresentation, well-corroborated

question: An 'innocent misrepresentation' -- a false statement of material fact made without knowledge of its falsity and without intent to deceive -- typically entitles the injured party to seek:
choice_a: Rescission of the contract, but generally not the tort damages available for fraudulent (intentional) misrepresentation
choice_b: Automatic criminal prosecution of the person who made the statement
choice_c: Punitive damages identical to those available for fraud
choice_d: No remedy of any kind, since no intent to deceive existed
explanation: An innocent misrepresentation still permits the misled party to seek rescission (unwinding of the contract) because it lacked a genuine meeting of the minds based on accurate facts, but because there was no intentional or reckless deception, the more punitive tort remedies (such as damages for fraud) generally associated with intentional misrepresentation are typically not available.
source_note: General contract law -- innocent vs. fraudulent misrepresentation, well-corroborated

question: A contract signed only because one party used improper threats or coercion to overcome the other party's free will is voidable on the ground of:
choice_a: Duress
choice_b: Novation
choice_c: Accord and satisfaction
choice_d: Assignment
explanation: Duress occurs when one party uses improper threats, coercion, or force to compel the other party into a contract that party would not otherwise have entered freely; because genuine mutual assent is lacking, a contract induced by duress is voidable at the election of the coerced party.
source_note: General contract law -- duress, well-corroborated

question: Undue influence, as a basis to void or rescind a contract, most typically arises when:
choice_a: A party in a position of trust or confidence (such as a caregiver or fiduciary) improperly uses that relationship to overcome another, more vulnerable party's free will and independent judgment
choice_b: Two sophisticated business parties negotiate a hard bargain at arm's length
choice_c: A licensed attorney reviews a contract before signing
choice_d: A contract is simply unfavorable to one side in hindsight
explanation: Undue influence involves the improper use of a position of trust, confidence, or authority (such as a caregiver, fiduciary, or close family relationship) to substitute one party's will for another's genuine free choice -- a concern of particular relevance to real estate transactions involving elderly or otherwise vulnerable sellers who may be pressured by someone in a position of influence over them.
source_note: General contract law -- undue influence, well-corroborated

question: The doctrine of unconscionability allows a court to refuse to enforce a contract or contract clause when:
choice_a: The contract terms are so one-sided or oppressively unfair, often combined with unequal bargaining power or unfair surprise in how the terms were presented, that enforcement would shock the conscience
choice_b: One party simply regrets the deal after signing
choice_c: The contract was negotiated by two attorneys
choice_d: The property involved is worth more than $1 million
explanation: Unconscionability generally requires both a procedural element (such as unequal bargaining power, unfair surprise, or fine-print terms a party had no real opportunity to understand) and a substantive element (terms so one-sided or oppressive that enforcing them would be fundamentally unfair), allowing a court to refuse enforcement of the offending term or the contract as a whole.
source_note: General contract law -- unconscionability, well-corroborated

question: The parol evidence rule generally provides that, once parties have reduced their full agreement to a final, integrated written contract:
choice_a: Prior or contemporaneous oral or written statements that contradict or vary the written contract's terms are generally inadmissible to alter that written agreement
choice_b: Any verbal promise made afterward automatically overrides the written contract
choice_c: The written contract is presumed invalid unless a witness testifies about what was orally discussed
choice_d: Oral statements always take precedence over the signed writing
explanation: The parol evidence rule generally bars the introduction of prior or contemporaneous oral or written statements to contradict, vary, or add to the terms of a final, fully integrated written contract, on the theory that the parties intended the final writing to represent their complete agreement -- though exceptions exist, such as evidence offered to show fraud, mistake, ambiguity, or a later, separate modification.
source_note: General contract law -- parol evidence rule, well-corroborated

question: A novation, as distinguished from an assignment, occurs when:
choice_a: All original parties and a new party mutually agree to substitute a new party (or a new contract) in place of an original party's obligations, completely discharging the original party from further liability
choice_b: A party simply transfers its rights under a contract to a third party without releasing the transferring party from any duties
choice_c: A contract is canceled with no substitute agreement of any kind
choice_d: A party unilaterally decides to stop performing without anyone's consent
explanation: Unlike a mere assignment (which transfers contractual rights, and typically does not by itself relieve the assignor of underlying duties without the other party's consent), a novation requires the agreement of all parties involved -- the original two parties plus the incoming new party -- to substitute a new party or new obligation in place of the old one, fully discharging the original party's liability under the prior agreement.
source_note: General contract law -- novation vs. assignment, well-corroborated

question: A 'condition precedent' in a real estate contract refers to:
choice_a: An event that must occur (or a state of facts that must exist) before a party's duty to perform under the contract arises
choice_b: A clause that automatically voids the entire contract retroactively
choice_c: A penalty imposed on the buyer for closing early
choice_d: A requirement that only applies after the closing has already occurred
explanation: A condition precedent is an event or set of facts that must occur before a party's contractual duty to perform arises -- financing and inspection contingencies in a real estate contract are common examples, since the buyer's obligation to close is conditioned on first obtaining approved financing or completing due diligence within the stated periods.
source_note: General contract law -- condition precedent, well-corroborated

question: Anticipatory repudiation (anticipatory breach) occurs when:
choice_a: A party clearly and unequivocally indicates, before performance is due, that it will not perform its contractual obligations, entitling the other party to treat the contract as breached immediately rather than waiting for the performance date to pass
choice_b: Both parties fully perform the contract exactly as agreed
choice_c: A party performs a few days early
choice_d: A contract is rescinded by mutual agreement before either party performs
explanation: Anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party clearly communicates -- through words or conduct -- that it will not perform its obligations once due, allowing the non-repudiating party to treat the contract as breached immediately, seek remedies without waiting for the performance date, and generally suspend or discontinue its own performance.
source_note: General contract law -- anticipatory repudiation, well-corroborated

question: An 'accord and satisfaction' discharges a contractual obligation when:
choice_a: The parties agree to accept a different, substitute performance (the accord) in place of the original obligation, and that substitute performance is actually rendered (the satisfaction), thereby discharging the original duty
choice_b: One party simply forgets about the original obligation over time
choice_c: A court forces a party to perform against its will
choice_d: The statute of limitations expires with no action taken
explanation: An accord is an agreement to accept some different performance from what was originally owed in satisfaction of an existing obligation, and satisfaction is the actual performance of that substitute agreement; once satisfaction occurs, the original obligation is discharged -- a doctrine sometimes seen in negotiated settlements of disputed debts or damages.
source_note: General contract law -- accord and satisfaction, well-corroborated

question: The doctrine of impossibility of performance (or frustration of purpose) may discharge a party's contractual duty when:
choice_a: An unforeseen event, occurring after formation and without either party's fault, makes performance objectively impossible or destroys the fundamental purpose of the contract
choice_b: A party simply finds performance less profitable than expected
choice_c: A party changes its mind for purely personal reasons
choice_d: Interest rates rise after the contract is signed
explanation: Impossibility of performance (and the related doctrine of frustration of purpose) may excuse a party from performing where an unforeseen event arising after contract formation, through no fault of either party, makes performance objectively impossible or destroys the fundamental purpose both parties understood the contract to serve -- mere increased cost, inconvenience, or reduced profitability generally does not rise to this level.
source_note: General contract law -- impossibility of performance / frustration of purpose, well-corroborated

question: A third-party beneficiary contract creates enforceable rights for a non-signing third party when:
choice_a: The third party is an 'intended beneficiary' whom the contracting parties specifically meant to benefit, as distinguished from a merely 'incidental beneficiary' who benefits only coincidentally
choice_b: Any person who happens to benefit indirectly from a contract automatically gains full rights to sue on it
choice_c: The third party co-signs the contract itself
choice_d: The contract is recorded in the public records
explanation: Only an 'intended beneficiary' -- a third party the contracting parties specifically meant to directly benefit from their agreement -- generally acquires enforceable rights under the contract; a merely 'incidental beneficiary,' who benefits only as a coincidental side effect of the contract without the parties intending to confer that benefit, generally has no right to enforce it.
source_note: General contract law -- third-party beneficiary contracts, well-corroborated

question: The equitable, quasi-contractual remedy of 'quantum meruit' (or unjust enrichment) generally allows recovery when:
choice_a: No valid, enforceable contract governs the situation, but one party has conferred a measurable benefit on another party who would be unjustly enriched by retaining it without paying for its reasonable value
choice_b: A fully valid written contract already specifies the exact price owed
choice_c: Both parties agree the contract is fair and fully performed
choice_d: A party wishes to recover punitive damages for fraud
explanation: Quantum meruit is a quasi-contractual (implied-in-law) remedy allowing recovery of the reasonable value of services or benefits conferred when no valid, enforceable express contract governs the parties' relationship, to prevent one party from being unjustly enriched at another's expense -- it is not a substitute for enforcing an actual valid contract that already fixes the price.
source_note: General contract law -- quantum meruit / unjust enrichment (quasi-contract), well-corroborated

question: Under Section 95.11(2)(b), F.S., an action for breach of a written contract in Florida must generally be brought within:
choice_a: 5 years
choice_b: 1 year
choice_c: 20 years
choice_d: 6 months
explanation: Section 95.11(2)(b), F.S., sets Florida's general statute of limitations for a legal or equitable action founded on a written contract at 5 years, generally running from the date of the breach rather than the date the breach is discovered.
source_note: Section 95.11(2)(b), F.S. (statute of limitations, written contracts)

question: Under Section 95.11(3)(j), F.S., an action for breach of an oral (unwritten) contract in Florida must generally be brought within:
choice_a: 4 years
choice_b: 10 years
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: There is no limitations period for oral contracts
explanation: Section 95.11(3)(j), F.S., sets Florida's general statute of limitations for a legal or equitable action founded on an oral (unwritten) contract at 4 years -- one year shorter than the 5-year period applicable to written contracts under Section 95.11(2)(b), F.S.
source_note: Section 95.11(3)(j), F.S. (statute of limitations, oral/unwritten contracts)

question: An 'implied-in-fact' contract, as distinguished from an express contract, is one in which:
choice_a: The parties' agreement is shown by their conduct and the surrounding circumstances rather than by explicit spoken or written words, even though a legally binding agreement is still formed
choice_b: No agreement of any kind exists between the parties
choice_c: The agreement must always be recorded in the public records to be valid
choice_d: One party is legally incapable of contracting
explanation: An express contract is formed through the parties' explicit spoken or written words, while an implied-in-fact contract is formed through the parties' conduct and the surrounding circumstances demonstrating mutual assent -- both are true, legally enforceable contracts; only a quasi-contract (implied-in-law) is not a true contract but an equitable remedy imposed to prevent unjust enrichment.
source_note: General contract law -- express vs. implied-in-fact contracts, well-corroborated

question: Under Florida's Statute of Frauds, Section 725.01, F.S., a lease of real property must be in writing to be enforceable if the lease term is:
choice_a: Longer than 1 year
choice_b: Any length at all, including month-to-month tenancies
choice_c: Longer than 10 years only
choice_d: Never required to be in writing under Florida law
explanation: Section 725.01, F.S., requires a lease of lands, tenements, or hereditaments for a period longer than 1 year to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged in order to be enforceable; shorter-term leases (1 year or less) are not subject to this particular writing requirement, though a written lease is still generally good practice.
source_note: Section 725.01, F.S. (Statute of Frauds -- leases exceeding 1 year)

question: Under Florida's Statute of Frauds, Section 725.01, F.S., a writing is required for an agreement that, by its own terms:
choice_a: Is not to be performed within the space of 1 year from the date the agreement was made
choice_b: Involves any amount of money whatsoever, no matter how small
choice_c: Is entered into between family members
choice_d: Concerns the sale of any item of personal property, regardless of value
explanation: Section 725.01, F.S., requires a writing for any agreement that, by its own terms, is not to be performed within 1 year from the date the agreement was made -- a category of Florida's Statute of Frauds separate from, but often discussed alongside, the writing requirement for real property sale contracts and leases exceeding 1 year.
source_note: Section 725.01, F.S. (Statute of Frauds -- agreements not performable within 1 year)

question: Under Florida's Statute of Frauds, Section 725.01, F.S., a promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another person (i.e., a suretyship or guaranty agreement) is enforceable only if:
choice_a: It is in writing and signed by the party to be charged (the person making the promise to answer for the other's debt)
choice_b: It is made verbally in front of at least two witnesses, with no writing needed
choice_c: It is recorded with the county property appraiser
choice_d: The original debtor also personally co-signs the guarantor's promise
explanation: Section 725.01, F.S., requires that a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another person -- a suretyship or guaranty arrangement -- be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (the guarantor) in order to be enforceable, just as with Florida's other statute of frauds categories.
source_note: Section 725.01, F.S. (Statute of Frauds -- promise to answer for debt of another)

question: Florida's Statute of Frauds requirement that a writing be 'signed by the party to be charged' means that, to enforce a contract against a particular party:
choice_a: Only that party's own signature is required by the statute, even though both parties typically sign a real estate contract for it to be mutually enforceable
choice_b: Both parties' signatures are irrelevant, since a verbal agreement alone always satisfies the statute
choice_c: Only the real estate licensee's signature is required, not either principal's
choice_d: A notary's signature alone satisfies the statute even without either party signing
explanation: Section 725.01, F.S., by its literal terms requires the writing to be 'signed by the party to be charged' -- meaning only the signature of the party against whom enforcement is sought is technically required by the statute for that party to be bound; in ordinary real estate practice, however, both buyer and seller sign the contract so that either party can enforce it against the other.
source_note: Section 725.01, F.S. (Statute of Frauds -- 'signed by the party to be charged')

question: Florida courts recognize a narrow 'partial performance' exception to the Statute of Frauds for an otherwise unwritten real estate sale agreement when a buyer seeks specific performance and can show, among other elements, that the buyer:
choice_a: Took possession of the property and made valuable, permanent improvements with the seller's consent, in addition to paying all or part of the purchase price
choice_b: Simply verbally agreed to the price with no other conduct
choice_c: Sent a text message expressing interest in the property
choice_d: Is seeking only monetary damages, not conveyance of the property
explanation: Florida recognizes a limited partial performance exception permitting specific performance of an otherwise unenforceable oral real estate agreement where the buyer has paid all or part of the consideration, taken possession of the property, and made valuable and permanent improvements with the seller's consent, with the oral agreement's terms proven by clear, definite, and certain evidence; this exception applies only where specific performance (conveyance) is sought, not to a claim for money damages alone.
source_note: Florida case law -- partial performance exception to the Statute of Frauds, Section 725.01, F.S.

question: Section 687.0304, F.S., Florida's statute of frauds for 'credit agreements,' provides that a debtor may not maintain an action on a credit agreement (an agreement to lend money, extend credit, or forbear repayment) unless the agreement:
choice_a: Is in writing, expresses consideration, sets forth the relevant terms and conditions, and is signed by both the creditor and the debtor
choice_b: Is made verbally between the lender and a loan officer, with no writing required
choice_c: Involves a Florida-licensed real estate broker as a witness
choice_d: Is recorded in the official public records of the county
explanation: Section 687.0304, F.S., requires that a credit agreement be in writing, express consideration, set forth the relevant terms and conditions, and be signed by both the creditor and the debtor in order for the debtor to maintain an action on it; the statute further specifies that a credit agreement may not be implied merely from the parties' relationship, whether fiduciary or otherwise.
source_note: Section 687.0304, F.S. (credit agreement statute of frauds)

question: Section 687.0304, F.S., specifically provides that a credit agreement between a lender and a borrower:
choice_a: May not be implied from the parties' relationship, whether fiduciary or otherwise -- it must satisfy the statute's writing requirements to be enforceable
choice_b: May always be implied automatically from a long banking relationship, without any writing
choice_c: Requires no consideration if the lender is a federally chartered bank
choice_d: Applies only to agreements exceeding $1 million
explanation: Section 687.0304(3), F.S., expressly states that a credit agreement may not be implied from the relationship, fiduciary or otherwise, of the creditor and the debtor -- reinforcing that only a properly executed written agreement meeting the statute's requirements (writing, consideration, terms, and both parties' signatures) can be enforced as a credit agreement in Florida.
source_note: Section 687.0304(3), F.S. (credit agreements may not be implied)

question: When a buyer submits a counteroffer in response to a seller's real estate contract offer, the legal effect is that:
choice_a: The buyer's counteroffer rejects and terminates the seller's original offer, and becomes a new offer that the seller may accept, reject, or counter
choice_b: The seller's original offer remains open and binding regardless of the counteroffer
choice_c: Both the original offer and the counteroffer become simultaneously binding
choice_d: The transaction automatically terminates and cannot be revived
explanation: A counteroffer operates as a rejection of the original offer, terminating it, and simultaneously proposes new terms as a fresh offer -- meaning the original offeror (here, the seller) is no longer bound by their original terms and must decide whether to accept, reject, or further counter the buyer's new proposal.
source_note: General contract law -- counteroffers, well-corroborated

question: In the standard FAR/BAR residential contract, the 'Effective Date' -- from which contingency periods such as the inspection period and financing period typically run -- is generally defined as:
choice_a: The date when the last of the buyer and seller has signed or initialed the offer or final counteroffer, and that signing has been communicated or delivered
choice_b: The date the buyer first viewed the property
choice_c: The date the closing actually occurs
choice_d: The date the listing agreement was originally signed
explanation: The FAR/BAR contract defines the Effective Date as the date when the last of the buyer and seller has signed or initialed the offer (or final counteroffer) and that fact has been communicated or delivered to the other party or their agent -- simply signing without delivery/communication does not, by itself, establish the Effective Date, which matters because deadlines like the inspection period, financing contingency, and closing date typically run from it.
source_note: Standard FAR/BAR contract 'Effective Date' provision, well-corroborated industry practice

question: An appraisal contingency in a real estate purchase contract generally protects the buyer by allowing the buyer to:
choice_a: Cancel the contract or renegotiate the price if the property's appraised value comes in below the agreed purchase price
choice_b: Force the seller to lower the price regardless of the appraisal result
choice_c: Automatically void the contract if the appraisal exceeds the purchase price
choice_d: Compel the appraiser to change the appraised value
explanation: An appraisal contingency allows a buyer to terminate the contract (and often recover the deposit) or attempt to renegotiate the purchase price or financing terms if the lender's appraisal of the property comes in below the agreed contract price, since many lenders will not finance more than the appraised value.
source_note: General real estate contract practice -- appraisal contingency, well-corroborated

question: A 'kick-out clause' in a real estate contract with a home-sale contingency (where the buyer's purchase is contingent on selling the buyer's current home) generally allows the seller to:
choice_a: Continue marketing the property and, upon receiving another acceptable offer, give the original buyer a specified window of time to remove the home-sale contingency or else the seller may terminate and accept the new offer
choice_b: Immediately cancel the contract the moment it is signed, with no notice to the buyer
choice_c: Refuse to show the property to any other prospective buyers under any circumstances
choice_d: Force the buyer's existing home to sell within 24 hours
explanation: A kick-out clause allows a seller who has accepted an offer contingent on the buyer selling their existing home to continue marketing the property; if the seller receives another acceptable offer, the seller gives the original buyer written notice and a specified period (commonly 24 to 72 hours) to either remove the home-sale contingency and proceed, or step aside and allow the seller to accept the competing offer, typically with the original buyer's deposit returned.
source_note: General real estate contract practice -- kick-out clause / home-sale contingency, well-corroborated
